section.title: Job Replies to Eliphaz
section.sectionRationale: Job answers Eliphaz's gentle counsel with a grief too heavy to be reasoned away. He accuses his friends of failing him like a dried-up desert stream, demands they show him his actual fault rather than assume one, and then, for the first time in the book, turns from talking about God to speaking directly to Him, a shift that will mark every speech Job gives from here on.
section.thesis: Job rejects Eliphaz's easy application of cause and effect, insists his complaint is justified given the weight of his suffering, and turns his grief into the book's first direct address to God, demanding to know why he is watched, tested, and not simply left alone.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the unbearable weight of Job's grief and his wish that God would finish him; his rebuke of his friends as unreliable as a seasonal desert stream; his challenge that they show him his actual error rather than assume one; his reflection on the hard service common to all mortal life; his first direct address to God, refusing to restrain his complaint; and his closing question, why does the watcher of mankind not simply look away.

units.label: The weight of my grief
units.note: the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me

verses.text: Then Job replied:
"If only my grief could be weighed and placed with my calamity on the scales.
For then it would outweigh the sand of the seas; no wonder my words have been rash.

For the arrows of the {{shadday|Almighty}} have pierced me; my spirit drinks in their poison; 
the terrors of God are arrayed against me.
Does a wild donkey bray over fresh grass, or an ox low over its fodder?
Is tasteless food eaten without salt, or is there flavor in the white of an egg?
My soul refuses to touch them; they are loathsome food to me.
If only my request were granted and God would fulfill my hope:
that God would be willing to crush me, to unleash His hand and cut me off!
It still brings me comfort, and joy through unrelenting pain, that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
What strength do I have, that I should still hope? What is my future, that I should be patient?
Is my strength like that of stone, or my flesh made of bronze?
Is there any help within me now that success is driven from me?

units.label: Faithless as a wadi
units.note: my brothers are as faithless as seasonal streams

verses.text: A despairing man should have the {{chesed|kindness}} of his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
But my brothers are as faithless as wadis, as seasonal streams that overflow,
darkened because of the ice and the inflow of melting snow,
but ceasing in the dry season and vanishing from their channels in the heat.
Caravans turn aside from their routes; they go into the wasteland and perish.
The caravans of Tema look for water; the travelers of Sheba hope to find it.
They are confounded because they had hoped; their arrival brings disappointment.
For now you are of no help; you see terror, and you are afraid.
Have I ever said, 'Give me something; offer me a bribe from your wealth;
deliver me from the hand of the enemy; redeem me from the grasp of the ruthless'?
Teach me, and I will be silent. Help me understand how I have erred.
How painful are honest words! But what does your argument prove?
Do you intend to correct my words, and treat as wind my cry of despair?
You would even cast lots for an orphan and barter away your friend.
But now, please look at me. Would I lie to your face?
Reconsider; do not be unjust. Reconsider, for my righteousness is at stake.
Is there iniquity on my tongue? Can my mouth not discern malice?

units.label: Man's hard service
units.note: months of futility, nights of misery

verses.text: "Is not man consigned to {{tsaba|labor}} on earth? Are not his days like those of a hired hand?
Like a slave he longs for shade; like a hireling he waits for his wages.
So I am allotted months of futility, and nights of misery are appointed me.
When I lie down I think: 'When will I get up?' But the night drags on, and I toss and turn until dawn.

My flesh is clothed with worms and encrusted with dirt; 
my skin is cracked and festering.
My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle; they come to an end without hope.
Remember that my life is but a breath. My eyes will never again see happiness.
The eye that beholds me will no longer see me. You will look for me, but I will be no more.
As a cloud vanishes and is gone, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come back up.
He never returns to his house; his place remembers him no more.

units.label: Job speaks directly to God
units.note: am I the sea, or the monster of the deep

verses.text:
Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; 
I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Am I the sea, or the {{tannin|monster of the deep}}, that You must keep me under guard?
When I think my bed will comfort me and my couch will ease my complaint,
then You frighten me with dreams and terrify me with visions,
so that I would prefer strangling and death over my life in this body.
I loathe my life! I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath.

units.label: What is man, that You test him every moment
units.note: why do You not pardon my transgression

verses.text: What is man that You should exalt him, that You should set Your heart upon him,
that You attend to him every morning, and test him every moment?
Will You never look away from me, or leave me alone to swallow my spittle?
If I have sinned, what have I done to You, O watcher of mankind? Why have You made me Your target, so that I am a burden to You?
Why do You not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For soon I will lie down in the dust; You will seek me, but I will be no more."

shadday.gloss: The Almighty, one of the most frequent divine names in Job. Job uses it here of the very arrows piercing him, the same overwhelming power his friends will invoke to argue God's justice always fits His actions to a person's conduct.

chesed.gloss: Loyal love, steadfast kindness, often used of covenant faithfulness between God and His people, or between friends. Job says a despairing man deserves this from his friend even if he has strayed from proper reverence; the bitter irony is that his own friends withhold exactly this.

tsaba.gloss: Hard service, a term also used for military conscription or compulsory labor. Job describes all human life on earth this way, hard, assigned, wearying, and then describes his own days as an extreme, unrelieved version of that universal toil.

tannin.gloss: A sea monster or dragon, a figure of untamed chaos similar to Leviathan. Job asks God whether he is such a monster, needing to be watched and restrained, a bitter question about why God's attention toward him feels like surveillance of a threat rather than care for a person.

basic.context: Job answers Eliphaz by insisting his grief is heavier than the sand of the seas and that his rash words are understandable given the weight of what he carries. He rebukes his friends for failing him like a desert stream that promises water and delivers none, and challenges them to actually show him where he has erred instead of assuming he must have. He then reflects on the hard, wearying service common to all human life, and for the first time in the book turns to address God directly, asking why he is watched and tested every moment rather than simply left alone to die in peace.
basic.hermeneutics: This speech shows that lament and protest can coexist with genuine faith; Job says he has not denied the words of the Holy One even while wishing for death and accusing his friends of failure. His demand, teach me where I have erred, is a fair one given what the reader already knows, and his shift to addressing God directly marks real spiritual progress, even though the content of what he says to God is raw complaint rather than composed praise.
basic.originalLanguages: Job says a suffering man deserves chesed, loyal kindness, from his friend, and finds none. He describes ordinary human existence as tsaba, hard conscripted service, then intensifies that picture with his own unrelieved suffering. And he asks God whether he is a tannin, a sea monster, that needs to be watched and restrained, turning the language of cosmic chaos into a personal, wounded question.
basic.typology: Job's demand to know his specific fault, met with silence, anticipates every innocent sufferer's cry for an explanation that does not come on schedule. His turn to direct address of God, even in anger and complaint, models the kind of honest prayer that the Psalms will make a permanent feature of Israel's worship.
basic.christ: Job asks why God will not simply pardon his transgression and let him be; Christ is the answer to exactly that longing, securing pardon for real transgression through His own suffering, not by God looking away but by God Himself bearing the cost. Job's cry, why have You made me Your target, finds its deepest answer in a cross where God's own Son became, in a far greater sense, the target of judgment so that pardon could be given freely.
basic.god: God is presented here as relentlessly attentive, testing man every moment, which Job experiences as suffocating surveillance rather than comfort. The tension between God's care and God's apparent harshness is not resolved in this chapter; it is simply voiced, honestly, as a real question asked directly to God rather than merely about Him.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 8:4 asks a strikingly similar question, what is man that You are mindful of him, but in wonder rather than complaint; Lamentations 3:1-20 gives voice to comparable raw lament; Romans 8:33-34 answers Job's demand for pardon with the assurance that no one can bring a charge against God's elect.
basic.oneStory: Job's turn to direct address of God, however raw, is a hinge in the book: suffering that was spoken about now becomes suffering spoken to God. That shift, and Job's unanswered longing for pardon, anticipates the gospel's answer, a Mediator who both hears every honest complaint and secures the pardon Job could only ask for.

context.literary:
Job's first reply has three parts, and each has a different listener. Job 6:2 to 6:13 is addressed to no one in particular and describes his pain. Job 6:14 to 6:30 turns on the friends, with the image of the wadi at the centre, Job 6:15-20, and moves from accusation to appeal, 'Teach me, and I will be silent,' Job 6:24. Job 7:1 to 7:10 is a meditation on human life in general, which drifts into the first person. Then, at Job 7:11, the hinge, 'Therefore I will not restrain my mouth,' and from that point to the end of the chapter Job speaks to God. The movement from friends to God is the structure of the speech, and it will be the structure of the book.

The poet works with unmistakable care. The reply begins with a scale, Job 6:2, and ends with a dust grave, Job 7:21, so that a man's grief is weighed and his body is laid down. The imagery moves from the desert, the wild donkey and the caravans in chapter 6, to the household, the hired worker, the bed and the weaver's shuttle in chapter 7. The chapter also repeats the words 'my days' and 'my life is but a breath,' giving a refrain of frailty.

Job also answers Eliphaz point for point. Eliphaz said that resentment kills the fool, Job 5:2, and Job asks that his own resentment be weighed, Job 6:2. Eliphaz said that man is born to trouble, Job 5:7, and Job describes the drudgery of that trouble in Job 7:1-3. Eliphaz called suffering God's discipline, Job 5:17, and Job says God's arrows have pierced him, Job 6:4. Eliphaz said, 'we have investigated,' Job 5:27, and Job says, 'Help me understand how I have erred,' Job 6:24. Read in sequence, chapters 4 to 7 are a conversation, not two speeches.
context.historical:
Job's central image, the seasonal stream, belongs to the landscape he knows. A wadi in the eastern desert carries melt and rain in winter and spring and is dry stone in summer. Caravans that planned by its water find nothing and, as Job 6:18 says, 'go into the wasteland and perish.' The reference to 'the caravans of Tema' and 'the travelers of Sheba,' Job 6:19, names real trade routes. Tema was an oasis in northern Arabia, listed among the sons of Ishmael, Genesis 25:15, and Isaiah 21:14 calls on the dwellers of Tema to bring water for the thirsty. Do not confuse it with Eliphaz's Teman in Edom. The two names sound alike, and Job may be quietly turning a place of water and wisdom into an emblem of disappointment.

Hospitality and loyalty to friends were serious obligations in this world. To leave a man in trouble was a breach of a kind of covenant. A friend was to be loyal at all times, Proverbs 17:17, and Job's charge that his brothers have 'faithless' dealings rests on that conviction.

The language of labour in Job 7:1-2, the hired hand and the slave who longs for shade and wages, reflects a society built on day labour and bonded service. Job takes a familiar picture, that human life is drudgery until the evening, and makes it personal. The wish for a wage at the end is the wish of people whose day ended only when someone paid them, Deuteronomy 24:15.

The picture of death in Job 7:9-10, 'he who goes down to Sheol does not come back up,' fits the common Old Testament view of the grave as a place of no return, and it sits behind the psalmists' pleas to be saved from it, Psalm 39:12-13. Job's demand to be remembered, and his fear that God will look for him and find him gone, is set against that view.
context.canonical:
Job 6 and 7 stand within a long line of biblical prayers that speak to God in complaint. Psalm 38:2-4 says 'Your arrows have pierced me deeply,' language close to Job's 'arrows of the Almighty,' Job 6:4. Lamentations 3:12 says God 'set me as the target for His arrow,' a match for Job 7:20. Psalm 69:20 laments, 'I looked for sympathy, but there was none, for comforters, but I found no one,' as Job says of his friends.

The most direct canonical link is Psalm 8. That psalm says, 'What is man that You are mindful of him,' and Job 7:17-18 turns it inside out: 'What is man that You should exalt him... that You attend to him every morning?' The psalm wonders that God notices a small creature; Job wonders that God cannot stop noticing. The letter to the Hebrews later quotes Psalm 8 of Jesus, Hebrews 2:6-9, and so completes a line that Job's parody bends.

The book of Job keeps the friends' arguments and Job's replies in an ongoing conversation that reaches into later wisdom books. Ecclesiastes holds the same sense of life as breath, hevel, and Job's 'my days are but a breath,' Job 7:16, uses the very word. The New Testament sums up the outcome: James points to Job's endurance and to the Lord's compassion, James 5:11.

Job's request for pardon in Job 7:21, 'Why do You not pardon my transgression,' uses the vocabulary of God's own self-description in Exodus 34:6-7, 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin.' Job asks God to be what God says He is. The gospel answers that plea at the cross, Colossians 2:13-14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted hearers to see what a good answer to bad comfort looks like. Job does not agree with Eliphaz, and he does not simply reject him either. He answers with a claim about the weight of his pain, a claim about the failure of loyalty, and a request to be shown his fault. Each is fair, and together they establish Job as a man who reasons honestly even in agony.

The author also meant to show that Job's honesty about his inner state was not a departure from faith. In Job 6:10 Job says his comfort is that he has 'not denied the words of the Holy One.' Hearers who had thought of faith as composure were to learn that a man can say 'I loathe my life,' Job 7:16, and still hold to the word of God. That distinction runs through the book.

Finally the chapter shows the point at which a sufferer stops explaining and starts praying. Job 7:11 is the hinge on which the book turns from a debate among men to a case between a man and God. Hearers are meant to notice that the address to God is angry, and that it is still address.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Job 6 and 7 record a suffering man's speech. Job's wish that God would crush him, Job 6:9, his description of God as a watcher who will not look away, and his request to be left alone, Job 7:19, are what he said, not what God requires. Nor should the picture of God as target-setter be taken as a settled doctrine of God: it is Job's perception, and the book will correct it.

At the same time the chapter gives a real allowance. Believers may bring their bitterness to God without translating it into theology first. Job's 'I will complain in the bitterness of my soul,' Job 7:11, is not rebuked. It is answered, in the end, with a meeting.

The chapter also carries a demand for friends. Job says 'a despairing man should have the kindness of his friend,' Job 6:14, and that is a norm. Believers owe each other chesed, and the failure of the friends in Job is a warning. The chapter does not say that all comfort fails or that people should stop offering it. It says that comfort must be loyal, honest and willing to be corrected, and it asks those who comfort to be teachable when the sufferer says, 'Show me where I have erred.'

debates.question: Is Job's wish for death in this chapter sinful despair, or legitimate lament?

views.label: Legitimate lament within the bounds of faith
views.case: Job says in Job 6:10 that he has not denied the words of the Holy One, even while wishing for death, and the narrator's verdicts in Job 1:22 and Job 2:10 have not been reversed. He asks God for death, not takes it himself, so his wish is prayer and not action.

views.label: The edge of what faith can bear, without yet crossing into sin
views.case: The intensity of Job's language, wishing God would crush him, sets up God's later question, 'Who is this who obscures My counsel by words without knowledge?' Job 38:2. The chapter may be the beginning of a drift, even if it does not itself cross the line.

debates.bearing: Whichever reading is preferred, the chapter treats Job's raw honesty as an ongoing part of his faith. Anyone who finds themselves wishing for death should hear Job as permission to speak, not as encouragement to stay silent about it, and should tell someone.

debates.question: How should Job 7:17-18 be read against Psalm 8?

views.label: A bitter parody that turns a hymn of wonder into a complaint
views.case: The Hebrew of Job 7:17-18 shares key words with Psalm 8:4, 'what is man,' and the verb 'attend to,' but reverses the mood. In the psalm God's attention is an honour; in Job it is a burden, since it comes every morning and tests him every moment. The parody is a way of saying that God's regard has become unbearable.

views.label: A sincere wonder that has been darkened by pain
views.case: Job may not be mocking at all. He genuinely marvels that God takes so close an interest in a human being, and his pain makes that interest feel like pressure. The wonder is intact; only the tone has changed.

views.label: An echo of a shared tradition, not a direct dependence
views.case: Some caution that the phrase 'what is man' is a common question of Israel's wisdom and worship, Psalm 144:3, and that the book of Job need not be quoting Psalm 8 at all. What matters is the shared question, whether God's attention to humans is grace or scrutiny.

debates.bearing: On any of these readings the passage shows that the same words can be praise or complaint depending on the state of the speaker. Hebrews 2:6-9 uses Psalm 8 in its hopeful sense, applied to Jesus.

debates.question: How does Job 6:14 read, and what does it say about the friends?

views.label: Kindness is owed even to a man who has abandoned the fear of God
views.case: The BSB reads, 'A despairing man should have the kindness of his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty.' Loyalty does not depend on the sufferer's spiritual state. This makes the friends' behaviour worse: even if Job were guilty, they owed him chesed.

views.label: Kindness is owed lest the despairing man abandon the fear of God
views.case: Some take the Hebrew as a purpose, so that kindness from a friend is what keeps a despairing person from forsaking the fear of the Almighty. On this reading the friends' failure endangers Job's faith, and their coldness is not just unkind but spiritually careless.

debates.bearing: The grammar of the verse is compressed and both readings are possible. Both make the same point about the friends, and both are consistent with the wider testimony that friendship is a serious duty, Proverbs 17:17.

study.originalLanguages:
Job's first word about his pain is ka'as, in Job 6:2, 'If only my grief could be weighed.' The Hebrew word can mean vexation, provocation or anger as well as grief. It is the word Eliphaz used in Job 5:2, when he said 'resentment kills a fool.' Job takes the word from Eliphaz's mouth and turns it back: weigh my ka'as, and see whether a man in that state is a fool for speaking as he does.

The word for the 'poison' Job's spirit drinks in Job 6:4 is chemah, which is also the word for heat and wrath. Whether Job means poison or fury, the point is that the arrows of the Almighty, chitsei Shaddai, do not only wound; they infect. In Job 6:10 he says that his comfort is that he has 'not denied' the words of the Holy One. The verb is kachad, to hide or deny, and it is the verb Joshua used to Achan, 'do not hide it from me,' Joshua 7:19. Job says that whatever else he has done, he has not concealed or disowned God's word.

The image of the wadi begins with the word bagad. Job says his brothers are 'faithless,' bagedu, like a stream. Bagad is the verb of betrayal, used of breaking covenant and marriage vows, so that the friends are charged with treachery and not merely disappointment. In Job 6:25 Job describes honest words, imre yosher, as painful, using the noun yosher, uprightness, which Eliphaz used of Job in Job 4:6. In Job 6:29 Job says 'Reconsider,' shuvu, twice. The word means turn back, the language of repentance. The friends have urged Job to return to God, and Job tells them to turn back from their injustice.

Job 7:3 uses amal for 'misery': 'nights of misery are appointed me.' The word for toil and trouble runs through this section of the book. It appears in Job 3:10 when Job wishes the womb had hidden 'the sorrow' from his eyes, in Job 4:8 for the trouble sown and reaped, in Job 5:6-7 for the trouble man is born to, and in Job 7:3 for his nights. The word turns from a doctrine to a diary.

In Job 7:16 he says his days are a breath, hevel, the word that Ecclesiastes will make famous. In Job 7:7 he says life is ruach, wind or breath. Frailty is measured by breath.

The verbs in Job 7:17-18 are the surprise. 'Exalt' is gadal, to make great, and 'attend to' is paqad, to visit or to take account of. Psalm 8:4 uses the same paqad, 'the son of man that You care for him,' and Job takes it from an image of God's care to an image of God's inspection. Then in Job 7:20 God is notser ha'adam, 'watcher of mankind.' The verb natsar means to watch or guard, and Proverbs 24:12 uses it of the One 'who guards your life.' Job's word for God's protective keeping has become a word for surveillance. The BSB footnote to Job 7:20 notes that 'a burden to You' follows the ancient Greek translation, while the Hebrew text reads 'to myself,' and an old Jewish tradition lists this verse among a small number of places where scribes are said to have altered a phrase they found too bold to leave about God.

In Job 7:21 Job asks God to pardon, using nasa, to lift or carry away, and to take away iniquity, avon, and he names his 'transgression,' pesha. These are the very words of Exodus 34:7, 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin.' The demand for pardon is a demand that God be who God has said He is.

typology.type: The arrows of the Almighty, Job 6:4
typology.fulfillment: Job feels God's arrows in him and believes the terrors of God are arrayed against him. In Christ the piercing is literal and purposeful: a soldier 'pierced His side with a spear,' John 19:34, and Zechariah's word, 'they will look on Me, the One they have pierced,' Zechariah 12:10, is applied to Him. Isaiah says He 'was pierced for our transgressions,' Isaiah 53:5. Where Job's arrows land on the innocent without a reason he can see, the arrows that hit Christ land in the place of the guilty. The type falls short since Job's perception is only partly true, and Christ's wound is the Father's plan.

typology.type: Friends who fail like a dry wadi, Job 6:15-20
typology.fulfillment: Job looked for sympathy and found streams that vanished. The Psalms voice the same complaint of a righteous sufferer: 'I looked for sympathy, but there was none,' Psalm 69:20, and in Gethsemane Jesus finds His disciples sleeping and asks, 'Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?' Matthew 26:40. The escalation is that Jesus is abandoned by all His friends, and still does not stop being faithful to them, John 13:1. He is also the answer to the dry stream: 'Whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst,' John 4:14. The type is an echo and not a strict prophecy.

typology.type: 'What is man?' turned inside out, Job 7:17-18
typology.fulfillment: Job reads Psalm 8's wonder as scrutiny. The letter to the Hebrews quotes the same psalm and answers it in Jesus: 'we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death,' Hebrews 2:6-9. The Man the psalm asks about is finally the Man who, by suffering, receives the honour God intended for humanity. Job's parody is set right in a single life. The correspondence has a limit: the psalm asks about the human race, and Hebrews shows Christ as its representative, so that His glory is offered to others.

typology.type: 'Why do You not pardon my transgression?' Job 7:21
typology.fulfillment: Job asks God to forgive, and cannot see how. The New Testament says the forgiveness is granted through a costly means: God 'forgave us all our trespasses, having canceled the debt ascribed to us,' and 'took it away, nailing it to the cross,' Colossians 2:13-14. The plea for God to be what He says He is, in Exodus 34:6-7, is met by a God who does not overlook sin and does not withhold pardon, because in Christ both are held together, Romans 3:23-26. The type falls short where Job's plea is made in ignorance of the means, and the gospel gives them.

study.christ:
Job 6 and 7 lead to Christ first by the sufferer's plea for pardon. Job asks, 'Why do You not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity?' Job 7:21, and he asks it with the words God used of Himself on Sinai. That is the deepest question in the chapter. If God is 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin,' Exodus 34:7, and yet 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished,' how are both true? The Old Testament holds the tension without resolving it. The gospel says that in Christ God acts 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26, and that the debt was nailed to the cross, Colossians 2:14. The plea of Job 7:21 is answered not by God looking away but by God bearing the cost.

It leads to Christ by the sense of being God's target. Job says God has made him a mark, Job 7:20. The Gospels tell of one who truly was the mark. The Father's will to 'crush Him,' Isaiah 53:10, fell on the Son, and the Son said, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' John 18:11. Job perceives that God is against him and is wrong; Jesus receives what God does against sin and is right. What is bitterness in Job is obedience in Christ. Yet the experience of being forsaken is real for both: Jesus cries, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46, which is Job's question in the mouth of one who did not deserve it.

It leads to Christ by the failed comforters. Job's brothers vanish like streams in the heat, and he says a despairing man should have the kindness of his friend. Jesus is deserted by all His friends in the garden, Matthew 26:40, and yet He does not forsake them. He is the friend who 'stays closer than a brother,' Proverbs 18:24, the one who gives His life for His friends, John 15:13. The friends of Job are a measure of what Job needed, and the Gospels say that in Christ he would have had it.

It leads to Christ by the picture of man under watch. Psalm 8 says that God is mindful of man. Job says God is a watcher of mankind who will not look away. Hebrews says that God's regard for humanity is finally seen in Jesus, who was made lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honour, Hebrews 2:9. The eye that Job finds oppressive is the eye that in Christ looks with grace on those who are in Him.

And it leads to Christ by the cry for a fair hearing. Job asks to be shown his fault, Job 6:24, and he will soon ask for a mediator, Job 9:32-33. The New Testament says, 'there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,' 1 Timothy 2:5. What Job could only wish for, the gospel announces.

A caution is needed. Job is not a picture of Christ's inner life, and his complaints contain things Christ could not have said, such as his wish to be cut off. The links above rest on the New Testament's own use of the themes of pardon, piercing, abandonment and mediation. What the chapter supplies is the hunger, and Christ is the answer to it.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who is addressed as a person and not a principle. From Job 7:11 Job speaks to God directly, and the address is angry, tired and honest. That fact alone says something about who God is: He is the kind of God to whom a man can say, 'Leave me alone,' Job 7:16, and who does not silence him for it. The Bible does not present a deity who requires politeness.

It shows a God who is intimately attentive. Job feels this as pressure, 'You attend to him every morning and test him every moment,' Job 7:18, but the same attention is the ground of every psalm of confidence. The God who watches mankind, Job 7:20, also 'guards your life,' Proverbs 24:12. The difference between surveillance and care lies in what the watching is for. Job cannot see the purpose, and the prologue has shown the reader that a purpose exists.

It shows a God who holds power over life and death. Job wants God to crush him, Job 6:9, and assumes that God is the one who could. This is an acknowledgment of sovereignty. Job does not ask the friends, or the enemy, or fate. He asks God, and that assumption is a form of faith even in its angriest form.

It shows the God of the covenant name and self-description. When Job asks for pardon in Job 7:21, he uses the vocabulary of Exodus 34:7. It means that even at his lowest Job knows who God has said He is, compassionate and forgiving, and holds Him to it. The God of Sinai has bound Himself to be that, and a sufferer can appeal to His own word.

It shows a God who does not defend Himself against a hurting man. The Almighty's silence in these chapters is not indifference, and the book will show that He answers. But here He lets Job speak. That patience is part of His character, and it teaches that God can be trusted with our unedited speech.

And it shows a God who is not the source of Job's friends' failure. They are 'faithless' as a wadi is faithless, and that failure is theirs. God is not the wadi. The contrast between the dry stream and 'the fountain of living water,' Jeremiah 2:13, suggests that what humans cannot supply in loyal comfort, God can.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to pray honestly. The whole of Job 7 is a prayer, though it does not sound like one, and God counts it as speech to Him. It also teaches us to hold on to what God has said about Himself when we cannot see what He is doing, as Job holds on to the words of the Holy One, Job 6:10. And it teaches congregations to make room for those whose prayer sounds like complaint.

crossReferences.note: Eliphaz said that resentment kills a fool, using the word ka'as. Job 6:2 takes up the same word when he asks for his own grief to be weighed. Reading them together shows Job answering Eliphaz line by line, and reveals that his reply is a defence against the charge of foolishness.

'What is man that You are mindful of him?' Job 7:17-18 uses the same question and the same verb for God's attention, but reverses the mood: what the psalm treats as honour, Job feels as inspection. The comparison shows how one question can be praise or complaint.

The letter quotes Psalm 8 and then points to Jesus, made lower than the angels and crowned with glory because He suffered death. It answers the question 'What is man?' that Job turns inside out, by giving a Man in whom God's purpose for humans is realised.

The righteous sufferer looked for sympathy and comforters and found no one. It matches Job's image of the failing friends in Job 6:15-21, and shows that the experience of being let down by friends belongs to the tradition of the faithful, not to the guilty.

'He bent His bow and set me as the target for His arrow.' The complaint is almost the same as Job 7:20, 'Why have You made me Your target?' Both voices see God as an archer aimed at them, and Lamentations also moves on to hope, Lamentations 3:21-23.

God's own description of Himself as forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin. Job 7:21 borrows this vocabulary when he asks why God does not pardon. He asks God to act as He has said He is, which is the strongest form of prayer.

'A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.' It states the norm that Job appeals to when he says a despairing man should have the kindness of his friend, Job 6:14. It also condemns the failure of the friends, who come in adversity and do not love.

'Your arrows have pierced me deeply.' The psalmist speaks of God's arrows and of a burden of sin too heavy to bear. The parallel to Job 6:4 shows that the image belongs to a shared language of suffering, though in the psalm the speaker links the arrows to his sin, and Job will not.

God is 'the fountain of living water,' and people who leave Him dig cisterns that cannot hold water. It offers a contrast with Job's dry wadi in Job 6:15-20: human sources of help fail, and God is the source that does not.

Job says God is not a man that he can answer, and there is no mediator between them. The wish for someone to 'lay his hand upon us both' takes up the need that Job 7 reveals, and points to 1 Timothy 2:5, where the mediator is named.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 ended with a man and a woman driven from God's presence and a world where labour is toil. Job 7 begins with that world: 'Is not man consigned to labor on earth? Are not his days like those of a hired hand?' Job 7:1. The cursed ground of Genesis 3:17-19 is in the background of every line, and so is the dust to which the human being returns, Job 7:21. The chapter also answers the question left hanging at the end of Genesis 3: can a person who lives under this curse still speak to God? Job's answer is that he can, and does.

Looking back, the chapter revisits the question of Psalm 8, what is man, from the far side of the fall. The dignity in the psalm, humanity crowned to rule creation, is what Job cannot feel. Instead he feels the frailty, the breath, the dust and the watch. The two views are held together in Scripture: the human being is at once a dignified image-bearer and a fragile creature of dust.

Looking forward, the chapter stands with the whole company of sufferers who pray in Scripture. The lament psalms, Jeremiah and Lamentations all speak to God in the same voice, and none of them is silenced. It also prepares for the greater questions of the book, the demand for a mediator, Job 9:32-33, the witness in heaven, Job 16:19, and the Redeemer who lives, Job 19:25. Job's plea for pardon in Job 7:21 opens a thread that reaches the cross.

The story finds its answer in Christ. The Man that Psalm 8 spoke of is Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honour, Hebrews 2:9. The God who watches is the God who came, and the piercing that Job felt as an arrow fell on the Son. The plea for pardon is answered in the blood, and the request for a mediator in the One Mediator, 1 Timothy 2:5.

In the new creation, Job's complaints are turned around. There will be no more toil like a hired hand's, but rest, and the nights of misery will be replaced by a city without night, Revelation 22:5. The God who watches will be seen face to face, Revelation 22:4. And the friend who is loyal in adversity, who never dries up like a wadi, will be with His people always. The chapter's questions are the questions of those who wait, and the story of Scripture tells how they are answered.

sermon.title: Miserable Comforters
sermon.why: Keller preaches on Job 5:1-7 and 6:1-10 together, examining the bad comfort of the friends and the better and ultimate comfort found only in Christ, directly addressing Job's rebuke of his friends as faithless as a dried-up desert stream.

quiz.q: Why does Job say his 'words have been rash' in 6:2-3?

options.text: Because his grief and calamity, if weighed, would outweigh the sand of the seas, making his intense words understandable given the scale of his suffering.
options.note: Job offers this as an explanation, not an excuse, for the intensity of his earlier lament in chapter 3.

options.text: Because the arrows of the Almighty have pierced him so deeply that his spirit itself drinks in their poison.
options.note: A true and vivid detail from the same passage, though less precise than his direct comparison of his grief to the weight of the sand of the seas.

options.text: Because he regrets rebuking his friends.
options.note: Job is about to rebuke his friends further, not retract an earlier rebuke; this misreads the sequence of the speech.

options.text: Because he now admits he was entirely wrong to speak at all.
options.note: Job defends the legitimacy of his complaint rather than retracting it.

quiz.q: What image does Job use to describe his friends' failure to comfort him?

options.text: A wadi, a seasonal desert stream that overflows with meltwater but vanishes exactly when travelers need water most.
options.note: This extended image in 6:15-20 captures how his friends' sympathy has proven unreliable when it mattered most.

options.text: A stream that promises relief but disappoints thirsty travelers when they finally reach it.
options.note: Captures the heart of the image, though less specific than naming the seasonal wadi and its meltwater origin directly.

options.text: A lion that roars but has no teeth.
options.note: This lion image appears earlier in Eliphaz's speech, 4:10-11, not in Job's rebuke of his friends here.

options.text: A well that never runs dry.
options.note: Job's image is the opposite, a stream that fails, not one that endures reliably.

quiz.q: What specific challenge does Job put to his friends in 6:24-30?

options.text: To actually teach him where he has erred, rather than simply assume guilt, since he insists his righteousness is at stake.
options.note: Job demands evidence, not assumption, echoing the reader's own knowledge that no such specific fault exists.

options.text: To stop treating his cry of despair as mere wind and actually engage his specific argument.
options.note: A true part of Job's challenge, though less precise than his direct demand that they identify his actual error.

options.text: To agree that all suffering is meaningless.
options.note: Job's challenge is specifically about identifying his own fault, not a broader claim about the meaninglessness of suffering.

options.text: To leave immediately and never return.
options.note: Job wants them to answer his challenge, not simply depart; he continues to engage them in dialogue for many more chapters.

quiz.q: What significant shift happens at Job 7:11?

options.text: Job turns from speaking about his situation to speaking directly to God for the first time in the book.
options.note: This marks a real development in Job's posture, moving from complaint about circumstances to direct, if raw, address of God Himself.

options.text: Job begins openly questioning why God watches him so closely, addressing his complaint toward God rather than only about Him.
options.note: Captures the substance of the shift, though less precise than naming it explicitly as Job's first direct address to God in the book.

options.text: The narrator interrupts with commentary on Job's words.
options.note: There is no narrator interruption here; the shift is within Job's own speech, from talking about God to talking to Him.

options.text: Job stops speaking entirely for the rest of the book.
options.note: Job continues to speak extensively throughout the following chapters.

quiz.q: What does Job's closing question in 7:20-21 reveal about his state of mind?

options.text: He longs for pardon and release, asking why God does not simply forgive whatever fault exists and leave him alone before he dies.
options.note: This closing plea combines Job's continued uncertainty about any specific fault with a genuine longing for mercy and rest.

options.text: He wishes God would simply stop testing him every moment and let him have a measure of peace before death.
options.note: A true part of Job's closing plea, though less complete than his explicit request for pardon of whatever iniquity exists.

options.text: He has abandoned belief that God hears him.
options.note: Job's direct address to God assumes God is listening even as he complains; this is not a statement of unbelief.

options.text: He is confident and at peace about his situation.
options.note: The chapter's tone throughout is one of anguish and complaint, not confidence or peace.

questions: Job says a suffering person deserves the loyal kindness, chesed, of a friend even if that person has strayed. Have you ever withheld kindness from someone because you first wanted to assess whether they deserved it?

Job compares his friends to a desert stream that promises water and delivers none exactly when it is needed most. Where have you disappointed someone in their hour of real need, even with good intentions?

For the first time in the book, Job turns from talking about God to talking directly to Him, even in complaint. What keeps you from bringing your rawest thoughts directly to God in prayer, rather than just thinking or talking about your situation?
Job demands evidence rather than assumption from his friends: teach me where I have erred. Where might you be assuming the cause of someone's suffering rather than actually asking or listening?

Job ends this speech longing simply to be pardoned and left in peace. What would it look like for you to bring an unresolved ache honestly before God this week, without needing to have the full explanation first?

translationNotes.note: Kindness renders chesed, a rich covenantal term for loyal love; Job's point is sharpened by the fact that this is exactly what his friends are failing to provide.
Labor renders tsaba, a term also used of military service or hard conscripted duty, casting all human life, not only Job's, as a kind of assigned hardship.

Monster of the deep renders tannin, a sea-dragon figure of chaos similar to Leviathan and Rahab elsewhere in the Old Testament; Job's question personalizes this cosmic image into a complaint about feeling watched like a threat rather than loved as a person.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Job 6:1-7:21. no other substantive changes were made to the verse text.
